lesson.title: 342 Chests in the Harbor: The Boston Tea Party
lesson.summary: In December 1773, Boston Patriots boarded three British ships and dumped a fortune in tea into the harbor rather than accept a tax they believed Parliament had no right to impose.
lesson.body:
For decades Britain had regulated colonial trade through the Navigation Acts, which required colonists to ship many goods on British vessels and through British ports and to route certain valuable products only to England. Colonists had learned to live with, and often quietly evade through smuggling, these older trade rules. Direct taxation was a different matter, and the Townshend Acts of the late 1760s had already taught Parliament that colonists would resist taxes imposed without their consent. Under colonial pressure, Parliament repealed most of the Townshend duties in 1770 but deliberately kept the tax on tea, in part to preserve the principle that Parliament had the authority to tax the colonies at all.

In 1773 Parliament passed the Tea Act, which was not meant to punish the colonies but to rescue the financially struggling British East India Company by letting it sell surplus tea directly to America, undercutting both colonial merchants and the smuggled Dutch tea many colonists had grown used to buying. Even though the new arrangement would have made legal tea cheaper for consumers, colonial leaders saw it as a trap. Accepting the tea, even at a lower price, meant accepting Parliament's right to tax them without representation, the very principle they had fought over during the Townshend Acts controversy just a few years earlier.

When tea ships arrived in Boston harbor in late 1773, Patriot leaders, including Samuel Adams and the Sons of Liberty, tried to pressure the royal governor, Thomas Hutchinson, into sending the ships back to Britain without unloading their cargo. Hutchinson refused, insisting the tea be landed and the duty paid. Colonists in other port cities, including Philadelphia and New York, managed to turn their own tea ships away or prevent the tea from being sold, but in Boston the standoff reached a breaking point.

On the night of December 16, 1773, a group of colonists, some thinly disguised as Mohawk Indians to signal that they acted as Americans rather than subjects of the crown, boarded three ships, the Dartmouth, the Eleanor, and the Beaver, docked at Griffin's Wharf. Working through the night, they broke open 342 chests of tea and dumped the contents into the harbor, destroying a cargo worth a considerable sum without harming the ships themselves or stealing anything for personal use. The disciplined nature of the destruction was itself a message: this was a deliberate political protest, not a riot or an act of theft.

News of the Tea Party spread quickly through the colonies and back to London, where it was received with outrage. Rather than seeing it as a protest against unjust taxation, King George III and Parliament viewed it as an act of vandalism and defiance that demanded a forceful response. That response would arrive the following year in the form of the Coercive Acts, laws so harsh that colonists would soon call them the Intolerable Acts, closing off any easy path back to the relative calm of the years before the Townshend Acts.
